DOC.EP: EC.01.01.01 The hospital plans activities to minimize risks in the environment of care. Note: One or more persons can be assigned to manage risks associated with the management plans described in this standard. EP 1. Leaders identify an individual(s) to manage risk, coordinate risk reduction activities in the physical environment, collect deficiency information, and disseminate summaries of actions and results. Note: Deficiencies include injuries, problems, or use errors.
DOC.FINDING: There has been a recent change in the Environment of Care Agenda and Minutes format as well as a new focus on attachments. However, the Data Management Program is still basically the collection of raw data with limited aggregation and analysis is difficult and at some times impossible. Some data is being presented in an improved format. Continue to standardize the data display that will markly improve the Committees' ability to track and trend data and to monitor Corrective Action Plan. The horizontal coordination, collaboration, communication and cooperation between Safety, Facilities and Infection Control has greatly improved.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The 2010 Annual Evaluations have been completed, but do not accurately represent the many accomplishments that have occurred in the environment of care for 2010. The plans, in may cases, reflect for the restatement of some of the Joint Commission standards. It is recommended that the Annual Evaluations be redone and not only cover specific accomplishments but include specific Goals for each plan for 2011. Also included should be specific and measurable Performance Improvement Measures for each plan. In the current evaluation, many for the measures were required activities, such as checking fire extinguisher monthly. Since this is not a problem, it should not be a primary measure. ? It is recommended that the Environment of Care Committee develop not only specific measurable goals/objectives, but include a specific timeline of completion, for each of the goals, for example Quarterly. The status and progress of the Goal should be monitored at least quarterly by the Environment of Care Committee. ? It is recommended that the Environment of Care Committee complete a Data Management Workshop related to the collection, aggregation, display and analysis. Also included, should how to develop and monitor Corrective Plans. ? An Annual Evaluation Template and samples of Performance Improvement Measures, by each plan are attached to this report. EP 4. The security of everyone who enters the hospital’s facilities. (See also EC.04.01.01, EP 15)
DOC.FINDING: Two Vendors were observed in the hospital without hospital required identification.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The hospital should determine the level security for Vendors, guests and families and implement and enforce those policies and procedures. EP 6. Fire safety. (See also EC.04.01.01, EP 15)
DOC.FINDING: During the Building Tour, penetrations were noted in smoke and fire partitions. Also during the Building Tour, three contractors were observed on the ground floor with ceiling tiles open in three different areas. One indicated he had never heard of contacting Facilities Management in advance of opening the ceiling. It was indicated by staff that passing Facilities Management is common. Identified violators included those sent by IT and the VISN. Both entities should be required to follow the established hospital policies and procedures.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Consider the immediate implementation of a Ceiling Permit Program. A copy was sent to the hospital with the May report and is attached to the report. The size of the hospital makes it almost impossible to assure a successful penetration repair program without controlling, 1100%, above ceiling work without advance approval and input from Facility Management. ? The Facility Manager must be given the authority to shutdown a project until the contractor follows established policies and procedures. EP 7. Medical equipment. (See also EC.04.01.01, EP 15) Time did not allow a review of this function There supervision of rental, loaned and borrowed equipment that comes to the hospital, particularly medical equipment supplied by vendors typically. A policy covering these situations was requested, but not received. ? A Rental, Loaned, Borrowed and Patient Owned Equipment Policy and Procedure should be developed and implemented if an effective program is not already in place.

DOC.EP: EC.02.01.01 The hospital manages safety and security risks. EP 1. The hospital identifies safety and security risks associated with the environment of care. Note: Risks are identified from internal sources such as ongoing monitoring of the environment, results of root cause analyses, results of annual proactive risk assessments of high-risk processes, and from credible external sources such as Sentinel Event Alerts. (See also

DOC.FINDING: A formal Security Risk Assessment has been completed for these areas.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The Risk Assessments, though basic will probably pass surveyor review. It is important that appropriate policies, procedures, plans and as appropriate, Performance Improvement Measures be implemented to support identified issues and weaknesses in these two programs. EP 7. The hospital identifies individuals entering its facilities. Note: The hospital determines which of those individuals require identification and how to do so. Though the hospital has strict security at the front door requiring the review of identification of all visitors, several vendors were noted that did not have a name tag. Three contractors were in the hospital doing cable work, but Facilities Management was aware that they were in the hospital. ? It is recommended that the Vendor and Contractor badge program be reviewed to assure that the policies and procedures are correct and are being strictly followed. ? Attention should be focused on assuring a clear and seamless coordination, communication, collaboration and cooperation between the Police Department and the Emergency Management Program. Being a member of the Emergency Management Committee does not assure that this will occur. EP 9. The hospital has written procedures to follow in the event of a security incident, including an infant or pediatric abduction. Two different Policies and Procedures, one Security and one for Emergency Management related to Infant/Child abduction. Neither were aware of the other Departments P/P. Though there is limited children in the facility it is recommended that a single Lost/Missing Child policy and procedure be incorporate in the Facility Lockdown Procedure. This should be drilled ASAP and fully critiqued.The Facility Lockdown Policy and Procedure was discussed with a representative of the Campus Police Department and the practice does not appear to include anyone outside of the Police Department in the event of a lost or possible abducted child. ? .Though there is limited children in the facility it is recommended that a single Lost/Missing Child policy and procedure be incorporate in the Facility Lockdown Procedure. This should be drilled ASAP and fully critiqued. ? More than the Campus Police Department should be involved in the event of an Infant/Child that is missing. This must be fully coordinated with the Facility Lockdown Procedure. This should be planned to manage a missing infant/child, 24/7. EP 10. When a security incident occurs, the hospital follows its identified procedures. Not related to a possible missing infant/child. ? It is recommended that an Aggregated Security Incident Report be sent to the Environment of Care Committee on a regular basis. ? The Police Department should make recommendations of what will be submitted, but the Committee should have final approval related to what will be reported, frequency and format.

DOC.EP: EC.02.01.03 The hospital prohibits smoking except in specific circumstances. EP 1. The hospital develops a written policy prohibiting smoking in all buildings. Exceptions for patients in specific circumstances are defined.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The hospital should be commended for their smoking enforcement program as the consultant did not find a single violation of this policy.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.01 The hospital manages fire risks. EP 4. The hospital maintains free and unobstructed access to all exits. Note: This requirement applies to all buildings classified as business occupancy. The "Life Safety" (LS) chapter addresses the requirements for all other occupancy types.
DOC.FINDING: Various halls, throughout the hospital that are used for primary egress, were found blocked by equipment, storage and clutter. This has been identified as an issue in various reports reviewed. The hospital certainly has a space problem, but this is a good example of items being identified as not in compliance, month after month, and the issue has not been resolved.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The hospital has a serious space problem and there must be a Senior Leadership directed approach to space management, to resolve blocked exits, alarm pulls, fire extinguishers and breaker panels. ? Just asking departments to move the equipment has not proven to be effective. The space problem should be reviewed in detail and a written master plan developed for: disposal of old and/or unused equipment and storage of equipment used intermittently. ? Assuring that all primary means of egress halls are clear and unobstructed, should be a top priority as this will result in multiple RFI's if not corrected.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.05 The hospital maintains fire safety equipment and fire safety building features. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the types of fire safety equipment and building features described below. However, if these types of equipment or features exist within the building, then the following maintenance, testing, and inspection requirements apply. EP 1. At least quarterly, the hospital tests supervisory signal devices (except valve tamper switches). The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2).
DOC.FINDING: This document review was much improved from the review conducted last May.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Some of the inspections were in process and/or had been scheduled and a completed evaluation could not be made. ? It is important that when a Life Safety deficiency or failure is identified by the company doing the inspection is noted and there is written evidence that the deficiency was not only corrected, but retested and the date. This is an important part of the documentation process. ? It is important that only the information requested by the Surveyor is submitted. Some of the books contained inspections conducted over 12 months ago. ? Another document review should be conducted with all that will be in attendance with the surveyor. A Surveyor Life Safety grid has been included to assist in this review. EP 2. Every 6 months, the hospital tests valve tamper switches and water-flow devices. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2). See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 3. Every 12 months, the hospital tests duct detectors, electromechanical releasing devices, heat detectors, manual fire alarm boxes, and smoke detectors. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2). See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 4. Every 12 months, the hospital tests visual and audible fire alarms, including speakers. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2). See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 5. Every quarter, the hospital tests fire alarm equipment for notifying off-site fire responders. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2). See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 6. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every week, the hospital tests fire pumps under no-flow conditions. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition. See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 7. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every 6 months, the hospital tests water-storage tank high- and low-water level alarms. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition (Section 6-3.5). See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 8. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every month during cold weather, the hospital tests water-storage tank temperature alarms. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition (Section 6-3). See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 9. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every 12 months, the hospital tests main drains at system low point or at all system risers. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition (Section 9-2.6). See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 10. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every quarter, the hospital inspects all fire department water supply connections. The completion dates of the inspections are documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition (Section 9-7.1). See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 11. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every 12 months, the hospital tests fire pumps under flow. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition. See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 12. Every 5 years, the hospital conducts water-flow tests for standpipe systems. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition. See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. ? See EC.02.03.05, EP 1, above. EP 13. Every 6 months, the hospital inspects any automatic fire- extinguishing systems in a kitchen. The completion dates of the inspections are documented. DOC.EP: EC.02.04.01 The hospital manages medical equipment risks. EP 2. The hospital maintains either a written inventory of all medical equipment or a written inventory of selected equipment categorized by physical risk associated with use (including all life-support equipment) and equipment incident history. The hospital evaluates new types of equipment before initial use to determine whether they should be included in the inventory. (See also EC.02.04.03, EPs 1 and 3)
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? A Loaned, Borrowed, Rental, Physical, Patient and Vendor furnished medical equipment Policy and Procedure should be developed and implemented as soon as possible. ? All medical equipment purchases should be coordinated with the Biomedical Department so they will be able to negotiate schematics and training program for staff, before the contract is signed and to assure the equipment is inspected before conducting patient care. ? Vendors bringing medical equipment into the hospital should notify the Biomedical Department before the equipment is demonstrated and/or used in patient care-no exceptions.

DOC.EP: EC.02.06.01 The hospital establishes and maintains a safe, functional environment. Note: The environment is constructed, arranged, and maintained to foster patient safety, provide facilities for diagnosis and treatment, and provide for special services appropriate to the needs of the community. EP 20. Areas used by patients are clean and free of offensive odors.
DOC.FINDING: The consultants noted numerous areas in the hospital that had horizontal dust. Examples include vending machines, offices and furniture and patient rooms. Corners in rest rooms were unclean and paper towel dispensers were packed so tightly towels could be removed only in pieces which were thrown on the floor or were empty. Base boards and bumper guards, particularly on the ground floor were dirty.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The coordination and communication of Infection Control and EMS does not appear to be effective nor ongoing.

DOC.EP: EC.02.06.05 The hospital manages its environment during demolition, renovation, or new construction to reduce risk to those in the organization. EP 2. When planning for demolition, construction, or renovation, the hospital conducts a preconstruction risk assessment for air quality requirements, infection control, utility requirements, noise, vibration, and other hazards that affect care, treatment, and services. Note: See LS.01.02.01 for information on fire safety procedures to implement during construction or renovation.
DOC.FINDING: The Infection Control Risk Assessment (ICRA) process was reviewed, but project documentation is not all in one project file and compliance is difficult to follow, particularly the actual ongoing inspections and documentation. There is no identification of who will conduct inspections, the frequency or who will maintain the data from the inspections. Inspections when Interim Life Safety Management (ILSM) is implemented are not consistently completed nor documented. Coordination, communication, cooperation and collaboration between Facility Management, Safety and Infection must be improved immediately. The ILSM application form is confusing to those that complete the form
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Construction and remodeling projects will always be underway and/or in the planning phase. Surveyors will look at the Infection Control Risk Assessment (ICRA), Interim Life Safety Management (ILSM), documentation of inspections and fire safety compliance will be a central focus of the Life Safety Surveyor. Documentation and coordination between departments must be outstanding to avoid various RFI's, some that will also be assigned under the Leadership Chapter which equals 2+ RFI's per deficiency. Documentation of all construction and remodeling projects, including inspections, should be reviewed at least twice in the next 60 days. ? The ICRA and ILSM forms should include a space for who, by title, should conduct inspections and the frequency of the inspections. Aggregation of the inspection results should be completed and regularly reported to the Environment of Care Committee. This is a serious deficiency and should be corrected immediately. An ILSM application template is attached to this report. EP 3. The hospital takes action based on its assessment to minimize risks during demolition, construction, or renovation. This will remain in non compliance until the consistency and quality of the inspections mentioned above is improved. ? Continue to refine and improve the process related to the ICRA and ILSM inspections until it is a seamless and effective process. Departmental silos, particularly between Facility Management and Safety are preventing the program from being effective. Infection Contorl should be more actively involved and focus should be more than just the ICRA.
